chapter: Young players, schools and studio work
title: Hinton on young Black musicians not knowing their history
summary: Hinton explains why Maxwell's oral history matters and asks why young Black musicians know little about Armstrong, Morton and Blanton.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Yeah. This is a continuation of that great session we were having talking with you. That's a beautiful story you were talking about there. And I just happened to mention to you in our conversation while we were setting up the tapes about some situations I'm sure you've been involved in and you've seen.

First, I'd just like to say that my conception of one of the reasons you are so much necessary for these archives is because of your great contribution to music and to jazz and your involvement, socially, with so many musicians of all colors and races. You're interested in languages, you're interested in people, and this kind of musician is certainly -- his records will certainly be read by future musicians, what it was like to be a musician and how it come about. Because sometimes we have to follow, we are what proceeded us in most cases. We build on our ancestors, our habit forming, our training. We may deviate and go in one special direction, but we are certainly influenced by them.
And I just happened to mention I have difficulty sometimes describing to young black musicians who don't know too much about their background, the younger ones nowadays, in the

seventies, doesn't seem too much interested. And I made the statement that now that so many of our greats have passed like Louis Armstrong and Charlie Shavers and Jelly Roll Morton and any number of greats, Jimmy Blanton, that many young blacks don't really know anything about them or even be too interested in learning.
And you made a statement to me about what you thought when you have run into that. Please, go on now.
